entities.summary:
Unilever, formed in 1929 through the merger of British soap maker Lever Brothers and Dutch margarine producer Margarine Unie, is one of the world's largest consumer goods companies with annual revenues of approximately €60 billion and approximately 400 brands sold in 190 countries. Unilever's products — from Dove soap to Lipton tea, Hellmann's mayonnaise to Ben & Jerry's ice cream — are present in the daily lives of 3.4 billion people globally, making it one of the world's most ubiquitous companies.

Lever Brothers was founded by William Hesketh Lever (later Lord Leverhulme) in 1885, who pioneered modern marketing, branding, and employee welfare: Port Sunlight, the model village he built for his soap workers in the Wirral, was one of industrial history's most ambitious experiments in corporate paternalism. Lever's Sunlight Soap brand created modern mass-market advertising. The 1929 merger with Margarine Unie created an Anglo-Dutch company with dual headquarters — one of the earliest multinational corporate structures.

Unilever's Sustainable Living Plan (2010) — committing to halve environmental footprint while doubling business — was the most ambitious corporate sustainability commitment of its era. CEO Paul Polman's refusal to provide quarterly earnings guidance (2009-2019) and his integration of environmental and social metrics into financial reporting created a corporate governance model widely emulated. Unilever's 2021 acquisition attempt of GlaxoSmithKline's consumer healthcare division for £50 billion was blocked by shareholders, exposing tensions between management's growth ambitions and investor returns.
